action_criteria.expected_evidence: Give-way weakness of arms and legs that becomes full with distraction, and an observed event of bilateral shaking with preserved awareness followed by a motionless phase with recall
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe the events
action_criteria.rationale: His limb weakness and his events are diagnosed by positive features (DSM-5 criterion B), and the examination separates them from the stocking sensory loss of his known diabetic neuropathy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Only a few punctate small vessel white matter hyperintensities, with no infarct, microhemorrhage or inflammatory lesion to suggest CNS vasculitis
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast for the CNS vasculitis question
action_criteria.rationale: New events at 64 in a man with a recent eosinophilic vasculitis, whose methotrexate was stopped for a suspected CNS inflammatory process: one non-contrast MRI with DWI, FLAIR and SWI answers that specific question once.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record the habitual events on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: Late-onset daily events treated with levetiracetam and diazepam without benefit: recording the habitual events without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level and is the basis for withdrawing levetiracetam (AAN 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Levetiracetam, started for the events, sedates with gabapentin and worsens mood, needs a gradual taper and renal dosing; gabapentin stays for the neuropathy
action_criteria.label: Review levetiracetam before withdrawal
action_criteria.rationale: Levetiracetam was started for misdiagnosed events and is to be withdrawn; the review checks its interaction with gabapentin, which he needs for his neuropathy, its mood effects and the pace of withdrawal.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies comorbid mood, anxiety and dissociation with performance-validity measures to plan treatment; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment
action_criteria.rationale: Optional: a battery would quantify his anxiety about the vasculitis, grief and caregiver strain for the treatment plan, but it does not make the diagnosis, which rests on the examination, and it is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on positive diagnosis and on physiotherapy and psychological therapy for FND; no step of this patient's work-up depends on it
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: A literature search is background reading, not a clinical step in this patient's pathway; it is optional and nothing required depends on it (ROUND_POLICY ruling 5).

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures, or stop it abruptly.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
Treat the events as CNS vasculitis with high-dose corticosteroids or cyclophosphamide.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional seizures, with functional limb weakness) based on the habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change, with preserved awareness during bilateral shaking, and the collapsing weakness that becomes full with distraction, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid anxiety about his vasculitis, with his grief and caregiver strain.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Taper and stop levetiracetam under neurological supervision, since the events are functional and there is no evidence of epilepsy; continue gabapentin for the diabetic neuropathy.
Ask rheumatology to review the treatment of the eosinophilic vasculitis, since methotrexate was stopped for a suspected CNS process that the work-up does not support.

avoided_actions.rationale: No structural cardiac question: heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation stayed normal during an observed event, and awareness was preserved.
His events are not syncope: vital signs were stable during an observed event with preserved awareness, and the events are recorded on video-EEG.
A CT adds nothing to the brain MRI that answers the vasculitis question.
FDG-PET has no role: the events have no ictal correlate and the MRI shows no inflammatory lesion.
His diabetic neuropathy is already established and the give-way weakness becomes full with distraction; EMG and nerve conduction answer no question about the events.
His stocking vibration loss is that of the known neuropathy; evoked potentials answer no question about the events.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder with psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES)

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures. Bilateral shaking with preserved awareness and a motionless phase with recall do not fit epileptic seizures.
The vasculitis raises the question, but the brain MRI shows no infarct, microhemorrhage or inflammatory lesion, there is no focal deficit or encephalopathy, and the events have no ictal change.
He reports palpitations, but heart rate 78, blood pressure 132/82 and SpO2 98% during an observed event, shaking up to 2 minutes with preserved awareness and immediate recall do not fit syncope.

differential.diagnosis: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy as the cause of the weakness
differential.key_features: Stocking vibration loss and 1+ ankle reflexes are those of his known neuropathy; proximal give-way weakness of all four limbs that becomes full with distraction is not.

key_clinical_evidence: Three habitual events, one seen during the examination, were recorded on 48-hour video-EEG without ictal change, with the posterior rhythm present during the motionless phase.
Semiology favours functional seizures: bilateral shaking with retained awareness, waxing and waning movements, a 2-minute motionless phase with recall, and stable vital signs.
Collapsing weakness of arms and legs becomes full with distraction; the stocking sensory loss and reduced ankle reflexes belong to his known diabetic neuropathy.
The non-contrast brain MRI shows only small vessel change, with no lesion of CNS vasculitis.
Levetiracetam, started for the events without benefit, is to be withdrawn gradually; gabapentin stays for the neuropathy.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A systemic vasculitis raises the question of CNS involvement, but the MRI shows no vasculitic lesion and the recorded events have no ictal change.
red_herrings.data_point: Eosinophilic vasculitis diagnosed 3 months ago, with methotrexate stopped for concern of a CNS inflammatory process
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the events to CNS vasculitis and escalate immunosuppression

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Punctate periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities at 64 with hypertension and diabetes are small vessel change, not vasculitis or demyelination.
red_herrings.data_point: A few punctate white matter hyperintensities on brain MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read the white matter change as CNS vasculitis and pursue angiography or biopsy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Vital signs were stable during an observed event and awareness was preserved; palpitations and transient toe cyanosis do not indicate syncope or hypoxia.
red_herrings.data_point: Palpitations with some episodes and transient toe cyanosis afterwards
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue a cardiac work-up for convulsive syncope

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Bereavement, caregiver burden and health anxiety are common context in FND but neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Death of his wife 18 months ago, care of his mother with dementia, and anxiety about his vasculitis
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treat the stressors as proof of FND without recording the events

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).
The decision to taper antiseizure drugs rests on the recorded events (AAN 2025; Oto 2005).

findings.result: Elbow flexion on both sides starts at 4+/5 and suddenly collapses; hip flexion and knee extension give way on both sides, more on the left.
Strength is full (5/5) in the same muscles when tested with distraction.
No pronator drift, wasting or fasciculation; reflexes 2+ except ankle reflexes 1+, plantar responses flexor; stocking loss of vibration at the toes.

A 45-second event that began with a pulsing sensation in both ears, then facial grimacing and leg tremor progressing to arrhythmic, waxing and waning shaking of all four limbs with the eyes open, followed by 2 minutes lying still with the eyes closed; he later reported full awareness throughout. Heart rate 78, blood pressure 132/82 and SpO2 98% during the event.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: collapsing weakness and distractibility. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (bilateral shaking with preserved awareness, waxing and waning movements, prolonged motionless phase with closed eyes and recall) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

contraindications: Sulfonamide allergy (rash): avoid sulfonamide-structured drugs, including the antiseizure drug zonisamide.
interactions: Levetiracetam with gabapentin: additive central nervous system depression (somnolence, dizziness, unsteadiness); no pharmacokinetic interaction.
Metformin and lisinopril: no clinically significant interaction with levetiracetam or gabapentin.
general.proposed: Metformin 1000 mg twice daily; Lisinopril 10 mg once daily; Gabapentin 300 mg three times daily; Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily
general.summary: Levetiracetam adds sedation to gabapentin and can worsen mood and anxiety; both drugs are renally cleared and should not be stopped abruptly; the sulfonamide allergy excludes zonisamide.
warnings: Levetiracetam: psychiatric and behavioral adverse effects (irritability, low mood, anxiety); withdraw by gradual dose reduction rather than abruptly.
Levetiracetam and gabapentin are renally cleared; adjust doses to creatinine clearance.
Gabapentin: abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal symptoms; reduce gradually if it is ever stopped.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed for 3 minutes, produced appropriate symmetric slowing, no abnormal discharges, did not provoke a clinical event
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Normal photic driving response at 10-20 Hz, no photoparoxysmal response

artifacts.note: Present during the clinical event; underlying cerebral rhythms were identifiable and normal

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 9.5 Hz symmetric alpha rhythm, well-modulated and reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_architecture: Normal sleep transients observed during drowsiness including vertex waves and K-complexes

findings.frequency: Day 1 during the neurological examination; shaking 45 seconds, then 2 minutes motionless
findings.morphology: Video shows facial grimacing and leg tremor progressing to arrhythmic shaking of all four limbs with eyes open. Muscle and movement artifact obscures frontal and temporal channels; posterior alpha rhythm is visible between artifact bursts. During the 2-minute motionless phase with eyes closed, a continuous 9.5 Hz posterior alpha rhythm is present. No ictal rhythm and no post-event slowing.
findings.type: Clinical event 1: generalized shaking followed by motionless unresponsiveness

findings.morphology: Similar event preceded by a reported ear sensation. Posterior alpha rhythm preserved; no ictal pattern; no post-event slowing.
Similar event while visitors were present. Posterior alpha rhythm preserved; no ictal pattern; no post-event slowing.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Three habitual events were recorded (arrhythmic shaking of all four limbs with eyes open, 45 to 110 seconds, the first followed by 2 minutes of motionless unresponsiveness with eyes closed) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Monitoring period 48 hours. Movement artifact during the shaking obscured frontal and temporal channels; posterior channels remained interpretable.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Gerald Novak is a 64-year-old right-handed Caucasian man who was transferred from an outside hospital to the neurology inpatient service for evaluation of recurrent seizure-like episodes over the past month. He was initially admitted to the outside facility after his primary care physician observed an episode of violent limb shaking during an office visit. At the outside hospital, levetiracetam was started empirically for suspected seizures and low-dose diazepam was administered during acute episodes, neither of which provided any benefit. He was also receiving methotrexate for a recently diagnosed eosinophilic vasculitis, which was discontinued prior to transfer due to concern for a possible CNS inflammatory process. The episodes are described as beginning with a pulsating sensation in both ears, followed by a wave of tension and pain radiating down his arms and legs, facial grimacing, and tremors of the lower extremities that rapidly escalate into violent bilateral shaking. He reports retaining full awareness throughout the shaking phase and can hear and understand those around him. He consistently denies loss of consciousness, tongue biting, or urinary incontinence. Each shaking event lasts between 30 seconds and 2 minutes and is followed by a period of approximately 2 minutes during which he lies motionless, appears unresponsive, but later reports complete awareness with an inability to move or speak. Transient peripheral cyanosis of the toes has been noted after some episodes. The events occur multiple times per day, predominantly in the presence of medical staff or visitors. His oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure have remained stable during and after each observed event. He reports palpitations coinciding with some episodes. His medical background is significant for type 2 diabetes with known peripheral neuropathy, hypertension, prior retinal detachment, and the recent eosinophilic vasculitis diagnosis. He lives alone following the death of his wife 18 months ago and is the primary caregiver for his elderly mother. He reports substantial psychological distress regarding his vasculitis diagnosis and ongoing anxiety about COVID-19 vaccination given his prior immunosuppressive therapy. He has become increasingly fearful of activity, spending most of his day in bed to avoid triggering episodes.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a witnessed episode lasting approximately 45 seconds. He first reported a pulsating sensation in his ears, followed by facial grimacing and bilateral lower extremity tremor that progressed to violent shaking of all four limbs. The shaking was arrhythmic, waxing and waning. His eyes were open but he appeared unresponsive. Vitals during the event were: HR 78, BP 132/82, SpO2 98%. After the shaking stopped, the patient lay still with eyes closed for approximately 2 minutes, during which he later reported he was fully aware but unable to move or speak. He denied loss of consciousness, tongue biting, and incontinence. Peripheral cyanosis of the toes was observed transiently. The episode self-resolved. Continuous EEG monitoring was in place during this event.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally without dysmetria or intention tremor. Heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Prior left retinal surgery noted but fundoscopic exam otherwise unremarkable, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or diplopia. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation, no facial weakness. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag reflex intact. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient was reluctant to ambulate, stating he might trigger an episode. When assisted to standing, gait was cautious but no focal abnormalities observed. No ataxia, no steppage gait, no Trendelenburg sign. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent with normal rate and rhythm. No dysarthria or aphasia. Attention intact, serial sevens performed without error. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. Affect mildly anxious with visible distress when discussing his illness. No thought disorder. Cooperative with examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in all extremities, no spasticity, rigidity, or cogwheel phenomenon. Upper extremities: inconsistent give-way weakness on bilateral elbow flexion, initially generating 4+/5 force then suddenly collapsing. Lower extremities: give-way weakness on bilateral hip flexion and knee extension, more pronounced on the left. Strength is full (5/5) when tested with distraction techniques. No pronator drift. No muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 1+ bilaterally (diminished, consistent with diabetic neuropathy). Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact in the upper extremities. Decreased vibration sense at the toes bilaterally consistent with known diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Proprioception intact at the great toes. No dermatomal or lateralized sensory loss beyond the expected stocking-pattern neuropathy.
